title: Watermarking Should Be Treated as a Monitoring Primitive
claim: Repeatedly linking outputs to a keyed source turns a hidden signal into surveillance, for insiders with detectors and outsiders without them.
layout: Left-to-right flow with purple internal and teal external observer bands; numbered governance levers
description: The figure is a horizontal flow diagram. On the left, a box for Entity e with key k_e feeds an arrow into a gray box, Watermarked model W_{k_e}. From there, four output boxes sit along a time axis: x1 service, x2 forum, x3 news site, and x4 anonymous post. A purple rounded band at the top is labeled Internal observer (detectors + key mapping). Arrows run up from each output into 'attributed to e' chips, which lead to 'observed activity of e'. A teal band at the bottom is labeled External observer (no keys or detectors). The known-account outputs x1 to x3 are bracketed as labeled outputs and feed a classifier f. The anonymous post x4 also feeds the classifier, which yields 'x4 identified as e'. Orange circled numbers 1 to 3 mark the governance levers: granularity, persistence and access. The eye goes first to the two colored observer bands.
caption: Repeated attribution turns a watermark into a monitoring primitive. An entity $e$ generates outputs under its key $k_e$, and the outputs appear beyond the provider's service. An internal observer with detectors and the key mapping attributes every output to $e$, which yields a record of $e$'s observed activity. An external observer without keys learns from outputs published under a known account and identifies the source of a later anonymous output. Orange numbers mark where governance acts, namely \lever{1} the granularity of key bindings, \lever{2} their persistence and \lever{3} access to detectors and the key mapping.
abstract: Watermarking is a primary means for providers of generative models to meet legal requirements to mark synthetic content. A watermark embeds a hidden signal into generated content that a detector holding a secret key can later recover. Its security is evaluated primarily against adversaries who remove or forge this signal in individual outputs. We argue that watermarking should also be evaluated and governed as a \emph{monitoring primitive}, because the same signal can link outputs to the entity that generated them. We show that (i) internal observers with detector access attribute outputs to individual entities even under zero-bit watermarks, which encode no identity, when each entity holds its own key, and (ii) external observers without keys or detectors identify the source of unseen text and image outputs in the configurations we test. Both depend on deployment choices that evaluations do not report, namely how fine-grained and persistent the bindings between keys and entities are and who may query the detector. We call for evaluations to report attribution and identification accuracy alongside robustness, and for governance to limit these bindings and detector access.
